newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Gold - demand eases, long-term view seen fair.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - demand eases, long-term view seen fair.

text.p: Demand for gold in Asia eased on Friday after the price swung back above US$320 per ounce but the long-term view for the metal remained fair, traders said.
"The demand is not so heavy today, gold prices were up more, so it's very quiet," a Hong Kong-based bullion supplier said on Friday.
Dealers said physical demand had been significant between $315 and $318 per ounce but buyers were now looking for lower levels nearer $300.

"Gold's sudden drop took physical buyers by surprise. They had even been buying at $340 per ounce thinking that was low and they were caught off-guard and so are more cautious now after the plunge," said one senior gold dealer. Gold prices dipped to a low of $313.60 on July 7 before rebounding and by Friday morning trade in Hong Kong had touched $320.50/321.00 per ounce.
Still, the steep decline in prices had boosted demand in Asia, and physical markets were seen remaining buoyant this year.
"If you talk to physical people, they're all pretty bullish. That is driven by the prices and buying," said a Hong Kong source.
Retail gold demand in Asia had picked up and was expected to remain firm over the next few weeks as people took advantage of the sharp slide in the price of the metal, dealers said.

"There's a mini-bull market among retailers right now. The retail side of the business has picked up because of the drop in gold prices," a senior jeweller in Singapore said. "The buying is going at a pretty good rate."
Demand ticked higher after gold plunged to near 12-year lows following a recent announcement that the Reserve Bank of Australia had sold 167 tonnes of the metal over the past few months.
One Singapore senior dealer said that despite the gold price drop, fresh buying in Southeast Asia had been limited by currency crises that had hit the Thai, Philippine and Malaysian economies.
In Cambodia, fighting between forces loyal to the country's rival co-prime ministers last weekend led to dealers re-routing gold destined there to other markets, dealers said.

Regional dealers predicted that the price of gold would stay in a narrow range between $315 to $320 an ounce over the next week or so, but may slide to the key $300 an ounce level in the coming months.
Brisk demand in Singapore helped keep premiums firm. They were quoted at a steady 70-75 U.S. cents an ounce over spot London prices, dealers said.
"The gold market is still bearish," said one senior Hong Kong source. He noted that fear of central bank sales still hung over prices, but that in the long term, Asian demand patterns may change.
"At the moment, much of the world's demand is in Asia, but economies are developing and investment patterns changing, and new tools are available for making money," he said.
He noted that although for the moment Asian central banks were conservative on gold sales, they could well jump into the fray.
